questions.questionText: Is it a way to describe the position of a point?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Let's rethink this one. Cartesian coordinates do describe point positions.

questions.questionText: So, it is a coordinate system?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Think it through.

questions.questionText: Does it use numbers as coordinates?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Yes! Points are described using numerical values along each axis.

questions.questionText: Does it describe a point using a Euclidean distance from the origin?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Nope—Cartesian coordinates use perpendicular axis values, not radial distance.

questions.questionText: Does it use angles to describe a point?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Maybe you got it confused with polar coordinates. Cartesian coordinates use perpendicular axes, not angles.

questions.questionText: Is it used in the 2D?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Yes! The Cartesian system is commonly used in 2D.

questions.questionText: Does it always require exactly two coordinates?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Not quite! While 2D requires two, Cartesian coordinates can also have just 1 dimension or extend into 3D or higher dimensions.

questions.questionText: Does a point always have a unique representation in this coordinate system?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Incorrect! Each point has one unique Cartesian coordinate representation.

questions.questionText: Are the axes mutually perpendicular?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Yes! By definition, Cartesian axes are perpendicular to one another.

terms.finalMessage: Looks like I figured it out! It's the Cartesian coordinate system!

questions.questionText: Is it a way to describe the positions of points?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Incorrect! Polar coordinates describe points using radius and angle.

questions.questionText: So, it is a coordinate system?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Think it through.

questions.questionText: Does it use only one coordinate for each point?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Nope—polar coordinates need both a distance (r) and an angle (θ).

questions.questionText: Does it use perpendicular axes generally labeled x and y?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Well... polar coordinates don’t use x and y axes but radius and angle.

questions.questionText: Does it use distance from the origin?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Yes! The first coordinate r is the distance from the origin.

questions.questionText: Does every point have exactly one representation?
questions.correctiveFeedback: If you think about it, (2, 0°) and (2, 360°) are two representations of the same point.

questions.questionText: Does it use angles to describe a point?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Yes! The second coordinate θ is an angle from the reference axis.

questions.questionText: Can it describe a circle more simply than Cartesian coordinates?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Exactly! Circles are easier in polar form: r = constant.

terms.finalMessage: Looks like I figured it out! It's the polar coordinate system!

questions.questionText: Is it a way to describe the positions of points?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Incorrect! Barycentric coordinates describe points' positions.

questions.questionText: So, it is a coordinate system?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Incorrect! Barycentric coordinates are a coordinate system.

questions.questionText: Does it measure distances from the x-axis and y-axis?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Nope—barycentric coordinates use weights relative to reference points, not axis distances.

questions.questionText: Does it use perpendicular axes?
questions.correctiveFeedback: This system uses reference points like triangle vertices instead of axes.

questions.questionText: Does it use reference points?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Yes! Barycentric coordinates are defined using reference points.

questions.questionText: Is it always used with 3 reference points?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Actually... we can use 2 points for a line, 3 for a plane, 4 for 3D space, etc.

questions.questionText: Can its coordinates in a plane be interpreted as weights of a triangle's vertices?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Well, they can! Each coordinate represents how much weight is placed on each vertex.

questions.questionText: Are the weights of triangle vertices always positive?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Remember, points outside the triangle can have negative barycentric coordinates.

questions.questionText: Can it be used to check if a point lies inside a triangle easily?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Simple rule: if all barycentric coordinates are between 0 and 1, the point lies inside.

questions.questionText: In this coordinate system, is the centroid of a triangle given by (½, ½, 0)?
questions.correctiveFeedback: Not quite! The centroid is found by averaging the vertices, so its coordinates are (⅓, ⅓, ⅓).

terms.finalMessage: Looks like I figured it out! It's the barycentric coordinate system!
